claim: PSI from different photosynthetic organisms has a variety of chlorophylls (Chls), some of which are at lower-energy levels than its reaction center P700.
source: PSI from different photosynthetic organisms has a variety of chlorophylls (Chls), some of which are at lower-energy levels than its reaction center P700, a special pair of Chls, and are called low-energy Chls.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of PSI.

claim: Low-energy chlorophylls in PSI are called low-energy Chls.
source: PSI from different photosynthetic organisms has a variety of chlorophylls (Chls), some of which are at lower-energy levels than its reaction center P700, a special pair of Chls, and are called low-energy Chls.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the abstract.

claim: The structure of PSI trimer from Gloeobacter violaceus PCC 7421 was solved at 2.04-Å resolution by cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, we solved a 2.04-Å resolution structure of a PSI trimer by cryo-electron microscopy from a primordial cyanobacterium Gloeobacter violaceus PCC 7421, which has no low-energy Chls.
evidence: The resolution and method are explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing described in the methods.

claim: Gloeobacter violaceus PCC 7421 has no low-energy Chls.
source: Here, we solved a 2.04-Å resolution structure of a PSI trimer by cryo-electron microscopy from a primordial cyanobacterium Gloeobacter violaceus PCC 7421, which has no low-energy Chls.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by fluorescence spectroscopy data showing absence of characteristic peaks at 723 or 730 nm.

claim: The Gloeobacter PSI structure shows the absence of some subunits commonly found in other cyanobacteria.
source: The structure shows the absence of some subunits commonly found in other cyanobacteria, confirming the primordial nature of this cyanobacterium.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis showing absence of PsaG, PsaH, PsaK, and PsaX.

claim: One dimeric and one trimeric Chls are lacking in the Gloeobacter PSI compared to PSI from other cyanobacteria and eukaryotic organisms.
source: Comparison with the known structures of PSI from other cyanobacteria and eukaryotic organisms reveals that one dimeric and one trimeric Chls are lacking in the Gloeobacter PSI.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The dimeric Chls absent in Gloeobacter PSI are named Low1.
source: The dimeric and trimeric Chls are named Low1 and Low2, respectively.
evidence: This naming is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: The trimeric Chls absent in Gloeobacter PSI are named Low2.
source: The dimeric and trimeric Chls are named Low1 and Low2, respectively.
evidence: This naming is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: Low2 is missing in some cyanobacterial and eukaryotic PSIs.
source: Low2 is missing in some cyanobacterial and eukaryotic PSIs, whereas Low1 is absent only in Gloeobacter.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons with multiple organisms.

claim: Low1 is absent only in Gloeobacter PSI.
source: Low2 is missing in some cyanobacterial and eukaryotic PSIs, whereas Low1 is absent only in Gloeobacter.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons showing Low1 presence in all other examined organisms.

claim: PSI functions in light-harvesting, charge-separation, and electron-transfer reactions.
source: PSI functions in light-harvesting, charge-separation, and electron-transfer reactions, leading to the reduction of NADP to NADPH required for CO2 fixation (Blankenship, 2021; Brettel and Leibl, 2001; Nelson and Yocum, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PSI leads to the reduction of NADP to NADPH required for CO2 fixation.
source: PSI functions in light-harvesting, charge-separation, and electron-transfer reactions, leading to the reduction of NADP to NADPH required for CO2 fixation (Blankenship, 2021; Brettel and Leibl, 2001; Nelson and Yocum, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PSI contains many cofactors, including chlorophylls (Chls), carotenoids (Cars), quinones, and iron–sulfur clusters.
source: PSI contains many cofactors, including chlorophylls (Chls), carotenoids (Cars), quinones, and iron–sulfur clusters, which serve in the photochemical reactions (Nelson and Yocum, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cyanobacterial PSI cores are present in either trimeric or tetrameric forms.
source: Among photosynthetic organisms, cyanobacteria are a large group of prokaryotes, and their PSI cores are present in either trimeric (Jordan et al., 2001; Malavath et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2020; Gisriel et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021) or tetrameric (Kato et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Semchonok et al., 2022) forms.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Cyanobacterial PSI complexes possess unique Chl molecules at energy levels lower than the level of P700.
source: Cyanobacterial PSI complexes also possess unique Chl molecules at energy levels lower than the level of P700, a special pair Chl that performs charge separation in each PSI-monomer unit (Brettel and Leibl, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Low-energy Chls are historically called red Chls.
source: The low-energy Chls are historically called red Chls, which differ in their energy levels among different species of cyanobacteria (Gobets and van Grondelle, 2001; Schlodder et al., 2005; Karapetyan et al., 2006; Schlodder et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The main functions of low-energy Chls in PSI are either uphill energy transfer from low-energy Chls to other Chls or excitation-energy quenching upon P700 oxidation.
source: The main functions of low-energy Chls in PSI are either uphill energy transfer from low-energy Chls to other Chls (Gobets and van Grondelle, 2001) or excitation-energy quenching upon P700 oxidation (Shubin et al., 1995; Shibata et al., 2010; Schlodder et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The locations of low-energy Chls in PSI are still under debate both experimentally and theoretically.
source: Despite numerous structural and functional analyses of the cyanobacterial PSI, the locations of low-energy Chls are still under debate both experimentally and theoretically (Gobets and van Grondelle, 2001; Schlodder et al., 2005; Karapetyan et al., 2006; Schlodder et al., 2007; Byrdin et al., 2002; Adolphs et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: It is very difficult to identify specific low-energy Chls from ~95 Chl molecules at different energy levels in a PSI monomer.
source: This is because it is very difficult to identify specific low-energy Chls from ~95 Chl molecules at different energy levels in a PSI monomer.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an explanation for the difficulty in identifying low-energy Chls.

claim: Two types of prominent fluorescence peaks from low-energy Chls appear at around 723 and 730 nm under liquid-nitrogen condition in PSI trimers from Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and Thermosynechococcus elongatus.
source: It is known that under the liquid-nitrogen condition, two types of prominent fluorescence peaks from low-energy Chls were mainly found. These two fluorescence peaks appear at around 723 and 730 nm in PSI trimers isolated from the representative cyanobacteria, Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 (hereafter referred to as Synechocystis) (van der Lee et al., 1993; Mimuro et al., 2010; Turconi et al., 1996) and Thermosynechococcus elongatus (Pålsson et al., 1996), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Gloeobacter violaceus PCC 7421 is a unique cyanobacterium that has no thylakoid membranes.
source: Gloeobacter violaceus PCC 7421 (hereafter referred to as Gloeobacter) is a unique cyanobacterium that has no thylakoid membranes, and its photosynthesis takes place in the cytoplasmic membranes similarly as that seen in anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (Guglielmi et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Photosynthesis in Gloeobacter takes place in the cytoplasmic membranes similarly as that seen in anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria.
source: Gloeobacter violaceus PCC 7421 (hereafter referred to as Gloeobacter) is a unique cyanobacterium that has no thylakoid membranes, and its photosynthesis takes place in the cytoplasmic membranes similarly as that seen in anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (Guglielmi et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Molecular phylogenetic analyses showed that Gloeobacter branched off from the main cyanobacterial tree at an early stage of evolution.
source: Molecular phylogenetic analyses showed that Gloeobacter branched off from the main cyanobacterial tree at an early stage of evolution (Nelissen et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Gloeobacter is considered as an evolutionary primordial cyanobacterium.
source: Therefore, Gloeobacter is considered as an evolutionary primordial cyanobacterium.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The Gloeobacter PSI did not exhibit characteristic fluorescence peaks at around 723 or 730 nm in fluorescence-emission spectra both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Unlike other cyanobacteria, the Gloeobacter PSI did not exhibit characteristic fluorescence peaks at around 723 or 730 nm in fluorescence-emission spectra both in vivo (Koenig and Schmidt, 1995) and in vitro (Mimuro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The final cryo-EM map of Gloeobacter PSI trimer with C3 symmetry enforced was determined at a resolution of 2.04 Å based on the 'gold standard' Fourier shell correlation (FSC) = 0.143 criterion.
source: After processing of the images with RELION (Appendix 1—figure 2 and Appendix 1—table 1), the final cryo-EM map with a C3 symmetry enforced was determined at a resolution of 2.04 Å, based on the 'gold standard' Fourier shell correlation (FSC) = 0.143 criterion (Figure 1A and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryo-EM data and FSC curve.

claim: The 2.04 Å resolution is the highest for the structure of PSI cores ever determined by X-ray crystallography and single-particle cryo-EM so far.
source: This resolution is the highest for the structure of PSI cores ever determined by X-ray crystallography and single-particle cryo-EM so far (Jordan et al., 2001; Malavath et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2020; Gisriel et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations to previous structures.

claim: The high resolution was realized by imaging with a cold-field emission electron beam that produces superior high-resolution signals.
source: This was realized by imaging with a cold-field emission electron beam that produces superior high-resolution signals (Hamaguchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The electron-transfer chain in Gloeobacter PSI consists of a special pair Chls P700, accessory Chl Acc, primary electron acceptor A0, secondary electron acceptor A1 (menaquinone-4), and three iron–sulfur clusters FX/FA/FB.
source: The components of the electron-transfer chain are assigned unambiguously, which consists of a special pair Chls P700, accessory Chl Acc, primary electron acceptor A0, secondary electron acceptor A1 (menaquinone-4), and three iron–sulfur clusters FX/FA/FB (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The densities for the Mg atoms in the Chl molecules are clearly visualized at their centers in the cryo-EM map.
source: The densities for the Mg atoms in the Chl molecules are clearly visualized at their centers (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: The characteristic structures of Chl a′ and Chl a that constitute the pair of P700 are distinguished clearly in the high-resolution map.
source: In addition, the characteristic structures of Chl a′ and Chl a that constitute the pair of P700 are distinguished clearly in the high-resolution map (red arrows in Figure 2B, C, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Menaquinone-4 has been detected in the Gloeobacter PSI core by HPLC.
source: On the other hand, menaquinone-4 is assigned here (Figure 2F) because it has been detected in the Gloeobacter PSI core by HPLC (Mimuro et al., 2005), although it is difficult to distinguish between menaquinone-4 and phylloquinone at the present resolution of the cryo-EM map due to the same length of their prenyl chain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: It is difficult to distinguish between menaquinone-4 and phylloquinone at the 2.04 Å resolution of the cryo-EM map due to the same length of their prenyl chain.
source: On the other hand, menaquinone-4 is assigned here (Figure 2F) because it has been detected in the Gloeobacter PSI core by HPLC (Mimuro et al., 2005), although it is difficult to distinguish between menaquinone-4 and phylloquinone at the present resolution of the cryo-EM map due to the same length of their prenyl chain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a limitation of the structural analysis.

claim: The electron-transfer chain is arranged in two branches approximately symmetrically in Gloeobacter PSI.
source: The electron-transfer chain is arranged in two branches approximately symmetrically, and no significant differences between the branches are found.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: It cannot be determined from the structure whether the electrons are transferred through both branches or proceed preferentially through one branch.
source: Thus, it cannot be determined if the electrons are transferred through both branches or proceed preferentially through one branch based on the structure obtained.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a limitation of structural interpretation.

claim: Each monomer of the Gloeobacter PSI contains 10 subunits.
source: Each monomer of the Gloeobacter PSI contains 10 subunits (Figure 1B), 9 of which are found in the genome of Gloeobacter (psaA, psaB, psaC, psaD, psaE, psaF, psaL, psaM, and psaZ) (Nakamura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nine subunits of Gloeobacter PSI (psaA, psaB, psaC, psaD, psaE, psaF, psaL, psaM, and psaZ) are found in the genome of Gloeobacter.
source: Each monomer of the Gloeobacter PSI contains 10 subunits (Figure 1B), 9 of which are found in the genome of Gloeobacter (psaA, psaB, psaC, psaD, psaE, psaF, psaL, psaM, and psaZ) (Nakamura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: PsaZ is positioned at the same location of PsaI in the PSI structure of Synechocystis.
source: PsaZ is positioned at the same location of PsaI in the PSI structure of Synechocystis (Malavath et al., 2018), although the Gloeobacter PsaZ has low sequence identity (20.0%) with the Synechocystis PsaI (Appendix 1—figure 3A, B; Inoue et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The Gloeobacter PsaZ has low sequence identity (20.0%) with the Synechocystis PsaI.
source: PsaZ is positioned at the same location of PsaI in the PSI structure of Synechocystis (Malavath et al., 2018), although the Gloeobacter PsaZ has low sequence identity (20.0%) with the Synechocystis PsaI (Appendix 1—figure 3A, B; Inoue et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The psaJ gene is not found in the Gloeobacter genome.
source: An additional subunit is found at the position of PsaJ, which was modeled as polyalanines (Appendix 1—figure 3C), because the psaJ gene is not found in the Gloeobacter genome (Nakamura et al., 2003) but a subunit is clearly visible in the map at the same position as PsaJ (Jordan et al., 2001; Malavath et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2020; Gisriel et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A subunit is clearly visible in the Gloeobacter PSI map at the same position as PsaJ in other cyanobacteria.
source: An additional subunit is found at the position of PsaJ, which was modeled as polyalanines (Appendix 1—figure 3C), because the psaJ gene is not found in the Gloeobacter genome (Nakamura et al., 2003) but a subunit is clearly visible in the map at the same position as PsaJ (Jordan et al., 2001; Malavath et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2020; Gisriel et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryo-EM map.

claim: The cryo-EM map of Gloeobacter PSI indicates the absence of PsaG, PsaH, PsaK, and PsaX found in other PSIs.
source: The cryo-EM map of Gloeobacter PSI indicates the absence of PsaG, PsaH, PsaK, and PsaX found in other PSIs, consistent with the absence of their genes in the Gloeobacter genome (Nakamura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The absence of PsaG, PsaH, PsaK, and PsaX in Gloeobacter PSI is consistent with the absence of their genes in the Gloeobacter genome.
source: The cryo-EM map of Gloeobacter PSI indicates the absence of PsaG, PsaH, PsaK, and PsaX found in other PSIs, consistent with the absence of their genes in the Gloeobacter genome (Nakamura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: PsaG and PsaH are absent in other cyanobacteria and appear in the green-lineage PSI cores.
source: While PsaG and PsaH are also absent in other cyanobacteria and appear in the green-lineage PSI cores, PsaK and PsaX are found in other cyanobacterial PSI structures (Suga and Shen, 2020; Jordan et al., 2001; Malavath et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2020; Gisriel et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: PsaK and PsaX are found in other cyanobacterial PSI structures.
source: While PsaG and PsaH are also absent in other cyanobacteria and appear in the green-lineage PSI cores, PsaK and PsaX are found in other cyanobacterial PSI structures (Suga and Shen, 2020; Jordan et al., 2001; Malavath et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2020; Gisriel et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The absence of PsaK and PsaX in the Gloeobacter PSI suggests that the PSI core from Gloeobacter is in an early stage of evolution before PsaK and PsaX are incorporated into PSI.
source: The absence of these subunits in the Gloeobacter PSI suggests that the PSI core from Gloeobacter is in an early stage of evolution before PsaK and PsaX are incorporated into PSI, and is consistent with the primordial nature of this cyanobacterium during the evolutionary process.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural data.

claim: The overall structures of PSI are largely similar among the cyanobacteria if some subunits that are absent or different between different cyanobacteria are not included.
source: This suggests that the overall structures of PSI are largely similar among the cyanobacteria, if we do not include some subunits that are absent or different between different cyanobacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RMSD comparisons.

claim: The Gloeobacter PSI possesses four types of characteristic loop structures named Loop1 (Tyr515–Gln529) and Loop2 (Asn652–Ser665) in PsaA, Loop3 (Pro717–Ile727) in PsaB, and Loop4 (Gln31–Asp36) in PsaF.
source: The Gloeobacter PSI possesses four types of characteristic loop structures which are named Loop1 (Tyr515–Gln529) and Loop2 (Asn652–Ser665) in PsaA (Appendix 1—figure 4), Loop3 (Pro717–Ile727) in PsaB (Appendix 1—figure 5), and Loop4 (Gln31–Asp36) in PsaF (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: These four types of loops do not exist in other cyanobacterial PSI trimers.
source: These four types of loops do not exist in other cyanobacterial PSI trimers (Jordan et al., 2001; Malavath et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2020; Gisriel et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: All loop insertions and deletions are located at the periplasmic side of the PSI monomer.
source: All these insertions and deletions are located at the periplasmic side of the PSI monomer (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There are 89 Chls a, 20 β-carotenes, 3 [4Fe–4S] clusters, 2 menaquinone-4s, and 4 lipid molecules in each monomer of Gloeobacter PSI.
source: The cofactors identified in the monomer unit of Gloeobacter PSI are summarized in Appendix 1—table 2. There are 89 Chls a, 20 β-carotenes, 3 [4Fe–4S] clusters, 2 menaquinone-4s, and 4 lipid molecules in each monomer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and summarized in a table.

claim: Six Chls are less in the Gloeobacter PSI than those in the T. vulcanus PSI and Synechocystis PSI.
source: The location of these molecules is similar to that in other cyanobacterial PSI structures (Jordan et al., 2001; Malavath et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2020; Gisriel et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021); however, six Chls are less in the Gloeobacter PSI than those in the T. vulcanus PSI (Akita et al., 2020) and Synechocystis PSI (Malavath et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The six missing Chls in Gloeobacter PSI include one Chl in PsaA (Chl1A), one Chl in PsaF (Chl1F), two Chls in PsaJ (Chl1J, 2J), and two Chls in PsaK (Chl1K, 2K).
source: These Chls include one Chl in PsaA (Chl1A), one Chl in PsaF (Chl1F), two Chls in PsaJ (Chl1J, 2J), and two Chls in PsaK (Chl1K, 2K) (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Both Chl1K and Chl2K do not exist in the Gloeobacter PSI because of the absence of PsaK in the genome and the structure.
source: Both Chl1K and Chl2K do not exist in the Gloeobacter PSI because of the absence of PsaK in the genome and the structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a direct consequence of PsaK absence.

claim: Chl1A is difficult to bind to the Gloeobacter PSI because the conserved His residue near Chl1A in other cyanobacteria is changed to Phe243 in the Gloeobacter PSI.
source: Chl1A is difficult to bind to the Gloeobacter PSI, because the conserved His residue near Chl1A in other cyanobacteria is changed to Phe243 in the Gloeobacter PSI (Appendix 1—figure 4 and Appendix 1—figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The change of His to Phe243 causes a steric hindrance between Phe243 and Chl1A in the Gloeobacter PSI, making the Chl molecule unable to bind.
source: This causes a steric hindrance between Phe243 and Chl1A in the Gloeobacter PSI (Figure 4D, Appendix 1—figure 7A), making the Chl molecule unable to bind.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Both T. vulcanus and H. hongdechloris PSIs possess an extra Chl (Chl1B) in PsaB which is absent in both Gloeobacter PSI and Synechocystis PSI.
source: In addition, it is interesting to note that both T. vulcanus and H. hongdechloris PSIs possess an extra Chl (Chl1B) in PsaB (Kato et al., 2020; Akita et al., 2020), which is absent in both Gloeobacter PSI and Synechocystis PSI (Malavath et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The absence of Chl1B in Gloeobacter and Synechocystis PSI is due to the changes in the loop structures.
source: This is due to the changes in the loop structures (Figure 4E, Appendix 1—figure 5), as suggested by Toporik et al., 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Chl1A forms a dimer with Chl2A in both Synechocystis PSI and T. vulcanus PSI.
source: Among the six Chl molecules that are absent in the Gloeobacter PSI mentioned above, Chl1A forms a dimer with Chl2A in both Synechocystis PSI (Figure 5A) and T. vulcanus PSI (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The Chl dimer of Chl1A and Chl2A may represent one of the low-energy Chls in most cyanobacteria other than Gloeobacter.
source: Thus, this Chl dimer may represent one of the low-energy Chls in most cyanobacteria other than Gloeobacter.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural comparison.

claim: The Mg atom of Chl1A is coordinated by a water molecule in the PSI structures of T. elongatus and H. hongdechloris.
source: The Mg atom of Chl1A is coordinated by a water molecule in the PSI structures of T. elongatus (Jordan et al., 2001) and H. hongdechloris (Kato et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: In T. elongatus, the water molecule coordinating Chl1A is hydrogen bonded to a neighboring His240.
source: In T. elongatus, this water molecule is hydrogen bonded to a neighboring His240 (Appendix 1—figure 7A), indicating that this hydrogen bond contributes to the stability of Chl1A.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The hydrogen bond between the water molecule and His240 contributes to the stability of Chl1A.
source: In T. elongatus, this water molecule is hydrogen bonded to a neighboring His240 (Appendix 1—figure 7A), indicating that this hydrogen bond contributes to the stability of Chl1A.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from structural analysis.

claim: His240 is conserved among most cyanobacteria but is changed to Phe243 in the Gloeobacter PsaA.
source: Sequence alignment showed that this His240 is conserved among most cyanobacteria (Appendix 1—figure 4); however, it is changed to Phe243 in the Gloeobacter PsaA (Appendix 1—figure 4 and Appendix 1—figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment.

claim: The change from His to Phe243 leads to the loss of the water molecule that can coordinate the Chl molecule.
source: As mentioned above, this change leads to the loss of the water molecule that can coordinate the Chl molecule (Appendix 1—figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from structural analysis.

claim: Both the His residue and water molecule are responsible for the binding of Chl1A.
source: Thus, both the His residue and water molecule are responsible for the binding of Chl1A.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from structural analysis.

claim: The Chl dimer of Chl1A and Chl2A found in the structure of most cyanobacterial PSI is named Low1.
source: Here, we name the Chl dimer of Chl1A and Chl2A found in the structure of most cyanobacterial PSI as Low1 (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: A trimeric Chl cluster of Chl1B/Chl2B/Chl3B is present in the T. vulcanus PSI but absent in the Gloeobacter and Synechocystis PSIs.
source: Further structural comparisons of T. vulcanus PSI with Gloeobacter PSI and Synechocystis PSI show a trimeric Chl cluster of Chl1B/Chl2B/Chl3B present in the T. vulcanus PSI but absent in the Gloeobacter and Synechocystis PSIs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparisons.

claim: The difference in the trimeric Chl cluster is due to the absence of Chl1B in Gloeobacter and Synechocystis.
source: The difference is due to the absence of Chl1B in the latter two cyanobacteria (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The Chl trimer of Chl1B/Chl2B/Chl3B is a probable candidate for low-energy Chls.
source: Therefore, this Chl trimer is also a probable candidate for low-energy Chls, which is supported by the spectroscopic analyses of PSI trimers (Schlodder et al., 2007) and the cryo-EM structure of PSI mutant complexes (Toporik et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The Chl trimer of Chl1B/Chl2B/Chl3B is named Low2.
source: Based on these findings, we name the Chl trimer of Chl1B/Chl2B/Chl3B as Low2 (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The spectrum of Synechocystis PSI exhibits a fluorescence peak at around 723 nm.
source: The spectrum of Synechocystis PSI (red line in Appendix 1—figure 8A) exhibits a fluorescence peak at around 723 nm, whereas that of T. vulcanus PSI (blue line in Appendix 1—figure 8A) displays a fluorescence peak at around 731 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Appendix 1—figure 8A.

claim: The spectrum of T. vulcanus PSI displays a fluorescence peak at around 731 nm.
source: The spectrum of Synechocystis PSI (red line in Appendix 1—figure 8A) exhibits a fluorescence peak at around 723 nm, whereas that of T. vulcanus PSI (blue line in Appendix 1—figure 8A) displays a fluorescence peak at around 731 nm.
